Life History Attributes Influencing Metabolic Variation in an Estuarine Fish

E. Hoots

2026-06-12

READ ME

All code and data analysis associated with “Life History Attributes Influencing Metabolic Variation in an Estuarine Fish” published in Functional Ecology in 2026. Authors: Hoots, Elizabeth; Kuchenmüller, Luis; Skeeles, Michael; Clark, Timothy

This analysis will explore the influence of energy allocated to growth on the baseline metabolism (standard metabolic rate or SMR) of juvenile fish. SMR is usually measured on fasted, postprandial, resting individuals, although in theoretical best practice it is also measured on a non-reproductive adult individual (no energy allocated to growth or maturation). In this study, I aim to study the relative influence of both growth and reproductive development on the baseline metabolism of Galaxias maculatus.

Read in data from Hoots et al. (2026) - hereafter “B1”

ds <- read.csv("001_Raw_Data/DS1_Hoots2026.csv") # read in data table

month_order <- c("April", "May", "June", "July", "August", "September", "November", "March") # assign chronological order to Month (otherwise alphabetical)
ds$Month <- factor(ds$Month, levels = month_order) # assign month_order to factor variable "Month" in ds

ds1 <- ds %>%  
  arrange(ID_fish, Month) %>%
  group_by(ID_fish) %>%
  mutate(mass_prev = lag(mass))

#month_order <- c("May", "June", "July", "August", "September", "November", "March") # assign chronological order to Month (otherwise alphabetical)
ds1$Month <- factor(ds1$Month, levels = month_order) # assign month_order to factor variable "Month" in ds1

ds1 <- ds1 %>%
  arrange(ID_fish, Month) %>%
  group_by(ID_fish) %>%
  mutate(SMR_prev = lag(SMR),
         MMR_prev = lag(MMR)) %>%
    ungroup() 


ds1 <- ds1 %>% 
  dplyr::mutate(
    Date = as.Date(time_start, format = "%d/%m/%Y")
  ) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(ds = "B1",
                ID = paste("B1",ID_fish, sep = "_"),
                Temp = as.factor(Temp_class),
                SMR_mass = NA,
                SMR_mass_prev = NA,
                MMR_mass = NA,
                MMR_mass_prev = NA) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(Temp = case_when(
    Temp == 18 ~ "18a",
    Temp == 23 ~ as.factor(23),
    .default = Temp
  )) %>%
  dplyr::select(ds, Month, Date, Temp, ID, mass, mass_prev, SGR, SMR, SMR_mass, SMR_resid, SMR_prev, SMR_mass_prev, MMR, MMR_mass, MMR_prev, MMR_mass_prev)

For this dataset, I also want to make an extra SGR calculation that spans a 2-month interval. This will allow me to make a comparison between “centred” SGR and metabolism later on.

ds1 <- ds1 %>%
  group_by(ID) %>%
  mutate(SGR_2m = (log(mass) - lag(log(mass), n = 2)) / as.numeric(difftime(Date, lag(Date, n = 2), units = "days")) * 100) %>%
  ungroup()

ds1 <- ds1[which(ds1$Month != "April"),] # subset a new table which excludes April, use if temp treatment matters or if not SGR

We are also interested in merging in some data on maturation in these fish, represented by the ratio between their gut and body cavity depth

#### let's also quickly take a look at those gut ratios 
B1_gut <- read.csv("001_Raw_Data/GutRatio.csv")

# Ensure Temp is correctly assigned
B1_gut <- B1_gut %>%
  mutate(
    Ratio = 100*Ratio,
    Rack = as.factor(Rack),
    Date = as.Date(Date, format = "%d/%m/%Y"),
    Julian = as.numeric(format(Date, "%j")),  # Convert Date to Julian day
    stage = as.factor(stage),
    ID = as.character(ID_fish),
    ID_fish = NULL,
    Temp = as.factor(case_when(Rack == 1 ~ as.factor("18a"), Rack == 3 ~ as.factor(23)))
  ) %>%
  mutate(ID = paste0("B1_", ID))

Relationship between SGR and mass for dataset B1:

This shows us a generally positive trend between SGR and mass, indicating that in general the biggest fish at any time point grew the most. This also shows us that there were no consistent fast or slow growers - rather there is a tangled web of fish jumping around in their growth levels throughout the experiment.

Gut ratio by individual across two measurements in August

ggplot(data=B1_gut, aes(x = Date, y = Ratio, color = Temp)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 74, linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +
  geom_line(aes(group = ID), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = Temp), method = "lm") +
  theme_bw() +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#78B7C5", "#F21A00")) +
  labs(color = expression("Temperature ("*degree*C*")"), y = "Gut to Body Depth Ratio (%)") +
  theme_classic()

This figure shows that fish at 23C generally did not mature in August, nor do they seem to have matured in July like the 18C fish did. It would be useful for the 18C fish to have a paired measurement of July SMR with gut ratio, which would help us understand whether a relationship exists between energy allocated to maturation and SMR.

Extrapolating measurements of gut ratio to correspond with July SMR measurements for 18C treatment fish only, as 23C fish were not found to have matured.

Using the gut ratio over time relationships established in Skeeles et al. (2023), we determined that a second-order polynomial model would be the best fit for these extrapolations. We start with a global model for each temperature treatment, then extrapolate individual-level values for their respective July respirometry trial dates based on their residuals from that global model.

To start, let’s generate a simple linear model to show (over)predicted gut ratio values as a comparison for some extrapolated quadratic model values:

# Define July dates
July <- ds1 %>% 
  filter(Temp == "18a") %>%
  filter(Month == "July") %>%
  dplyr::select("Date", "Temp", "ID")

# Fit individual regressions only for fish with at least two data points
gut_models <- B1_gut %>%
  group_by(ID) %>%
  filter(n() > 1) %>%  # Ensure at least two data points per fish
  summarise(
    model = list(lm(Ratio ~ Date, data = pick(everything())))
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# Predict values for July
gut_predictions <- July %>%
  left_join(gut_models, by = "ID") %>%
  mutate(
    Ratio = map2_dbl(model, Date, ~ if (!is.null(.x)) predict(.x, newdata = data.frame(Date = .y)) else NA_real_)
    ) %>%
  dplyr::select(ID, Date, Temp, Ratio)

# Combine with original data
B1_gut_linear <- bind_rows(
  B1_gut %>% dplyr::select(ID, Date, Temp, Ratio),
  gut_predictions
) %>% rename(
  Ratio_linear = Ratio
)

B1_gut_linear$ID <- as.character(B1_gut_linear$ID)

# Merge extrapolated data into ds1
ds1 <- ds1 %>% 
  left_join(B1_gut_linear %>% dplyr::select("ID", "Date", "Ratio_linear"), by = c("ID", "Date"), na_matches = "na")

Let’s visualize that now:

fig_line <- ggplot(B1_gut_linear[which(B1_gut_linear$"Temp" == "18a"),], aes(x = Date, y = Ratio_linear, color = Temp)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 74, color = "darkgrey", linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = ID), method = "lm", linewidth = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", se = FALSE) +
  geom_point(data = B1_gut_linear[which(B1_gut_linear$Temp == "18a"),], aes(x = Date, y = Ratio_linear, color = Temp), size = 1.5) +
  geom_point(data = gut_predictions[which(gut_predictions$Temp == "18a"),], aes(x = Date, y = Ratio), size = 2, shape = 21, fill = "white") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#78B7C5")) +
  labs(color = expression("Temperature ("*degree*C*")"), y = "Gut to Body Depth Ratio (%)") +
  theme_bw()

fig_line

Now we can get a bit fancier, and try using a more biologically accurate quadratic model:

# # # Fit global poly2 model (for trend)
global_model <- lm(Ratio ~ poly(Julian, 2), data = B1_gut)

# Get residuals (how each ID deviates from the trend)
B1_gut <- B1_gut %>%
  mutate(Residual = Ratio - predict(global_model, newdata = data.frame(Julian = Julian)))

# Extract individual July dates per fish - only in the 18C treatment
July_dates <- ds1 %>% 
  filter(Temp == "18a") %>%
  filter(Month == "July") %>%
  dplyr::select("Date", "Temp", "ID") %>%
  mutate(
    Julian = as.numeric(format(Date, "%j")),
    Global_Pred = predict(global_model, newdata = data.frame(Julian = Julian)),  # Global trend
    ID = as.character(ID))

# Adjust for individual residuals based on their own July date
gut_predictions <- B1_gut %>%
  filter(Temp == "18a") %>%
  group_by(ID) %>%
  summarise(Mean_Residual = mean(Residual, na.rm = TRUE), Temp = first(Temp)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  left_join(July_dates, by = c("ID", "Temp")) %>%
  mutate(
    Ratio = Global_Pred + Mean_Residual  # Adjusted extrapolation for each fish's date
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(ID, Date, Julian, Temp, Ratio)

# Combine observed data & adjusted extrapolated points
B1_gut_extrap <- bind_rows(
  B1_gut %>% mutate(ID = as.character(ID)) %>% dplyr::select(ID, Date, Temp, Ratio),
  gut_predictions
) %>%
  mutate(Julian = as.numeric(format(Date, "%j")))

B1_gut_extrap$ID <- as.character(B1_gut_extrap$ID)

# Merge extrapolated data into ds1
ds1 <- ds1 %>% 
  left_join(B1_gut_extrap %>% dplyr::select("ID", "Date", "Ratio"), by = c("ID", "Date"), na_matches = "na")

Let’s visualize that:

We have now extrapolated individual-level estimates for gut-to-body-depth ratio at the July respirometry trial dates, using each fish’s residuals from a global 2nd-order polynomial model. This follows the relationship found in Skeeles et al. (2023), as well as the timing of maturation and re-absorption of reproductive tissues - although this seems to have occurred on an accelerated timeline in these fish compared to Skeeles et al. (2023). These values do not differ greatly from what was seen using linear models to extrapolate, however the linear model predicted biologically unlikely gut ratio values near 100%, while this model does not.

# merge extrapolated data into ds1
ds1 <- ds1 %>% 
  left_join(B1_gut_extrap %>% dplyr::select("ID", "Date", "Ratio"), by = c("ID", "Date"), na_matches = "na") %>% 
  left_join(B1_gut_linear %>% dplyr::select("ID", "Date", "Ratio_linear"), by = c("ID", "Date"), na_matches = "na") %>% 
  mutate(Date = NULL,
         SGR_2m = lead(SGR_2m),
         Ratio = Ratio.x,
         Ratio_linear = Ratio_linear.x,
         Ratio.y = NULL,
         Ratio_linear.y = NULL,
         log_SMR = log10(SMR),
         log_MMR = log10(MMR),
         log_mass = log10(mass)) %>%
  dplyr::select(ds, Month, Temp, ID, mass, mass_prev, SGR, SGR_2m, SMR, SMR_mass, SMR_resid, SMR_prev, SMR_mass_prev, MMR, MMR_mass, MMR_prev, MMR_mass_prev, Ratio, Ratio_linear, log_SMR, log_MMR, log_mass)

read in data from Hoots et al., 2024 - hereafter “B2”

ds2 <- read.csv("001_Raw_Data/DS2_Hoots2024.csv")

#Note: SGR for November is calculated as % mass increase per day, from September to December (functionally centered). SGR for March is calculated from December to March, and thus is not centered or suitable for this analysis. 

ds2<- ds2 %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    ds = "B2",
    Month = as.factor(Month),
    Temp = as.factor("18b"), #as.factor(Temp)
    mass_prev = NA,
    SGR_2m = as.numeric(case_when(Month == "November" ~ SGR, Month == "March" ~ NA)) ,
    ID = paste("B2",ID, sep = "_"),
    mass_SMR = SMR_mass,
    SMR_resid = NA,
    SMR_mass = NA,
    SMR_mass_prev = NA,
    MMR_mass = NA,
    MMR_mass_prev = NA,
    log_SMR = log10(SMR),
    log_MMR = log10(MMR),
    log_mass = log10(mass),
    Ratio = NA,
    Ratio_linear = NA
  ) %>% 
  arrange(ID, Month) %>%
  group_by(ID) %>%
  mutate(mass_prev = lag(mass)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  dplyr::select(ds, Month, Temp, ID, mass, mass_prev, SGR, SGR_2m, SMR, SMR_mass, SMR_resid, SMR_prev, SMR_mass_prev, MMR, MMR_mass, MMR_prev, MMR_mass_prev, Ratio, Ratio_linear, log_SMR, log_MMR, log_mass)

merge 3 datasets into single master table

data <- bind_rows(ds1, ds2, ds3)

temp_order <- c(15, "18a", "18b", 20, 23) # assign chronological order to Temp (otherwise alphabetical)
data$Temp <- factor(data$Temp, levels = temp_order) # assign temp_order to factor variable "Temp" in ds1
data$Month <- factor(data$Month, levels = month_order) # assign month_order to factor variable "Month" in ds1


# summarise data for Functional Ecology replication statement:

# Count repeated measures per fish (this gives replication information for metabolism and mass)
fish_repeats <- data %>% #subset data by !is.na(SGR_2m) or !is.na(Ratio) for factor-specific replication information 
  group_by(ID) %>%
  summarise(
    n_measurements = n(),   # counts rows per fish
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Summarise across fish: mean ± SD of repeated measurements
summary_repeats <- fish_repeats %>%
  summarise(
    mean_reps = mean(n_measurements),
    sd_reps   = sd(n_measurements),
    min_reps  = min(n_measurements),
    max_reps  = max(n_measurements),
    n_fish    = n()
  )

# View results

data_factor <- data %>%

  filter(n() > 1) %>%
  summarise(
    factor_SMR = max(SMR_mass) / min(SMR_mass),
    range_SMR = max(SMR_mass) - min(SMR_mass),
    factor_MMR = max(MMR_mass) / min(MMR_mass),
    range_MMR = max(MMR_mass) - min(MMR_mass),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

We see a narrowing-in when we plot SMR vs. mass for our four temperatures. While mass-scaling intercepts tend to increase with temperature, slopes seem to decrease. This creates an effect where, for the largest fish, there is not a visible difference in SMR by temperature treatment - they have converged to what may be a mass-imposed metabolic floor.

fig2 <- ggplot(data = data, aes(x = mass, y = MMR, color = factor(Temp))) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = F) +
  theme_bw() +
  scale_color_manual(values =c("darkblue", "deepskyblue3", "skyblue", "orange", "orangered")) +
  labs(x = "Mass (g)", y = expression(MMR~(mg~O[2]~h^-1)), color = expression("Temperature ("*degree*C*")")) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  theme_classic()

fig2

# plot gut ratio vs. mass-standardized MMR, indicate extrapolated values:
fig6 <- ggplot() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 74, color = "grey", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_point(data = datamat, aes(x = Ratio, y = MMR_mass, color = factor(Temp)), shape = 21, size = 2) +
  geom_point(data = datamat[which(data$Month == "July"),], aes(x = Ratio, y = MMR_mass, color = factor(Temp)), shape = 21, fill = "white")+
  geom_smooth(data = datamat, aes(x = Ratio, y = MMR_mass, color = factor(Temp)), method = "lm", se = F) +
  scale_color_manual(values =c("deepskyblue3", "skyblue", "orange", "orangered"),
    guide = guide_legend()) +
  labs(x = "Gut Ratio (%)", y = expression(MMR~(mg~O[2]~h^-1~3.47~g^-1)), color = "Temperature") +
  theme_classic()

fig6

# gut ratio vs. mass-standardized MMR but using linearly extrapolated gut ratio values:
ggplot() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 74, color = "grey", linetype = "dashed", size = 1.5) +
  geom_point(data = datamat, aes(x = Ratio_linear, y = MMR_mass, color = factor(Temp))) +
  geom_point(data = datamat[which(data$Month == "July"),], aes(x = Ratio_linear, y = MMR_mass, color = factor(Temp)), shape = 21, fill = "white") +
  geom_smooth(data = datamat, aes(x = Ratio_linear, y = MMR_mass, color = factor(Temp)), method = "lm", se = F) +
  theme_bw() +
  scale_color_manual(values =c("darkblue", "skyblue3", "orange", "orangered")) +
  labs(x = "Gut Ratio (%)", y = expression(MMR~(mg~O[2]~h^-1~3.47~g^-1)), color = "Temperature")

Gut ratio really does not seem to have any correlation with mass-standardized SMR (any correlation seen between gut ratio and SMR could be explained by mass). Note that this figure uses the previously extrapolated values (above). For MMR, the case is a bit more complicated.

One way to explore this from a different perspective is to treat maturation as a binary state rather than a continuous variable. I will add a new column to data giving maturation status, and look for temperature-specific differences in SMR or MMR between the two states. Note that only 18C has a meaningful spread of data above and below the 0.74 threshold.

data_matstat <- data %>%
 mutate(matstat = case_when(
    Ratio >= 74 ~ "Mature", 
    Ratio < 74 ~ "Immature",
    is.na(Ratio) ~ NA,
    .default = "cusp")
  )

data_matstat_18 <- data_matstat[which(data_matstat$Temp == "18a" & !is.na(data_matstat$matstat)),] 

data_matstat_18_July <- data_matstat_18[which(data_matstat_18$Month == "July"),]

#visualize this as two boxplots, with a welch's t-test (due to unequal groups: 36 mature and 73 immature). separate by month to show chronological differences:
ggplot(aes(y = SMR_mass, x = matstat, colour = factor(matstat)), data = data_matstat_18) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter() +
  facet_grid(.~Month) +
  stat_welch_anova_test() +
  theme_bw()

# to run a proper pairwise test here, I need to also filter for only individuals which were mature in one month and immature in the other

data_matstat_18_diff <- data_matstat_18[which(data_matstat_18$ID != "B1_78"),] %>%
  group_by(ID) %>%
  mutate(changed = case_when(
    length(unique(matstat))==1 ~ "same",
    length(unique(matstat))==2 ~ "diff",
    .default = "same")
  )%>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(changed != "same") %>%
  mutate(
    changed = NULL
  ) 

data_matstat_18_smr <- data_matstat_18_diff %>% 
  dplyr::select(ID, SMR_mass, matstat) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = matstat, 
    values_from = c(SMR_mass)
    ) 

t_maturity_smr <- t.test(Pair(Mature, Immature) ~ 1, data = data_matstat_18_smr)
t_maturity_smr #shows that individuals have a significantly lower SMR_mass when mature than when immature/regressing
## 
##  Paired t-test
## 
## data:  Pair(Mature, Immature)
## t = -2.7051, df = 31, p-value = 0.01099
## alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  -0.12330061 -0.01729731
## sample estimates:
## mean difference 
##     -0.07029896
data_matstat_18_mmr <- data_matstat_18_diff %>% 
  dplyr::select(ID, MMR_mass, matstat) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = matstat, 
    values_from = c(MMR_mass)
    ) 

t_maturity_mmr <- t.test(Pair(Mature, Immature) ~ 1, data = data_matstat_18_mmr)
t_maturity_mmr #shows that individuals have a significantly lower MMR_mass when mature than when immature/regressing
## 
##  Paired t-test
## 
## data:  Pair(Mature, Immature)
## t = -4.363, df = 31, p-value = 0.000132
## alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  -0.3268271 -0.1186059
## sample estimates:
## mean difference 
##      -0.2227165
#grouped across month (but note that individuals are repeated twice):
ggplot(aes(y = SMR_mass, x = matstat, colour = factor(matstat)), data = data_matstat_18) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(aes(group = Month)) +
  theme_bw()

fig5_inset <- ggplot(aes(y = SMR_mass, x = matstat), data = data_matstat_18) +
  geom_boxplot(color = "skyblue") +
  geom_jitter(color = "skyblue") +
  #facet_grid(.~Month) +
  #stat_welch_anova_test() +
  labs(x = " ", y = expression(SMR~(mg~O[2]~h^-1~3.47~g^-1))) +
  theme_classic()

#addressing reviewer comment that changes in MMR between individuals might be of interest
ggplot(aes(y = MMR_mass, x = Month, colour = factor(matstat)), data = data_matstat_18) +
  geom_point() + 
  geom_line(aes(group = ID), color = "grey") +

We could then run a linear regression test between metabolism and gut ratio at 18:

data_matstat_18 <- data_matstat[which(data_matstat$Temp == "18a" & !is.na(data_matstat$matstat)),] 

lmod_SMR <- lmer(log(SMR_mass) ~ log(Ratio) + (1 | ID), data = data_matstat_18)
plot(lmod_SMR) 

summary(lmod_SMR)
## Linear mixed model fit by REML. t-tests use Satterthwaite's method [
## lmerModLmerTest]
## Formula: log(SMR_mass) ~ log(Ratio) + (1 | ID)
##    Data: data_matstat_18
## 
## REML criterion at convergence: -31.1
## 
## Scaled residuals: 
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -2.2606 -0.6143 -0.0439  0.5290  3.7382 
## 
## Random effects:
##  Groups   Name        Variance Std.Dev.
##  ID       (Intercept) 0.00000  0.0000  
##  Residual             0.04172  0.2043  
## Number of obs: 109, groups:  ID, 55
## 
## Fixed effects:
##             Estimate Std. Error       df t value Pr(>|t|)
## (Intercept)  -0.2179     0.6734 107.0000  -0.324    0.747
## log(Ratio)   -0.1142     0.1588 107.0000  -0.719    0.473
## 
## Correlation of Fixed Effects:
##            (Intr)
## log(Ratio) -1.000
## optimizer (nloptwrap) convergence code: 0 (OK)
## boundary (singular) fit: see help('isSingular')
anova(lmod_SMR)
## Type III Analysis of Variance Table with Satterthwaite's method
##              Sum Sq  Mean Sq NumDF DenDF F value Pr(>F)
## log(Ratio) 0.021597 0.021597     1   107  0.5177 0.4734
emm_SMR <- emtrends(lmod_SMR, ~1, var = "log(Ratio)")
emm_SMR
##  1       log(Ratio).trend    SE   df lower.CL upper.CL
##  overall           -0.114 0.161 97.4   -0.435    0.206
## 
## Degrees-of-freedom method: kenward-roger 
## Confidence level used: 0.95
performance::check_model(lmod_SMR, ask = F)
